passages.title: What is Photosynthesis
passages.text: Photosynthesis is the biochemical process by which green plants, algae and some bacteria convert light energy, usually from the sun, into chemical energy stored in glucose. It uses carbon dioxide and water as raw materials and releases oxygen as a by-product. Photosynthesis is the primary source of energy for almost all life on Earth and forms the base of most food chains.

passages.title: Photosynthesis Equation
passages.text: The overall balanced chemical equation of photosynthesis is 6CO2 + 6H2O + light energy -> C6H12O6 + 6O2. Six molecules of carbon dioxide combine with six molecules of water in the presence of light and chlorophyll to produce one molecule of glucose and six molecules of oxygen.

passages.title: Role of Chlorophyll
passages.text: Chlorophyll is the green pigment found in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy, mainly in the blue and red regions of the visible spectrum, and reflects green light, which gives plants their green colour. Chlorophyll a is the primary pigment while chlorophyll b, carotenoids and xanthophylls are accessory pigments that widen the range of light absorbed.

passages.title: The Chloroplast
passages.text: The chloroplast is the organelle where photosynthesis takes place. It contains stacks of thylakoid membranes called grana suspended in a fluid called the stroma. The thylakoid membranes hold chlorophyll and the machinery for the light-dependent reactions, while the stroma is the site of the Calvin cycle.

passages.title: Light-Dependent Reactions
passages.text: The light-dependent reactions occur in the thylakoid membranes. Light energy is absorbed by photosystems II and I, splitting water molecules in a process called photolysis to release oxygen, protons and electrons. This drives the production of ATP through photophosphorylation and NADPH, which are energy carriers used in the next stage.

passages.title: Light-Independent Reactions (Calvin Cycle)
passages.text: The Calvin cycle, also called the light-independent or dark reaction, takes place in the stroma of the chloroplast. It uses ATP and NADPH from the light reactions to fix carbon dioxide into organic molecules. The enzyme RuBisCO fixes CO2 to a 5-carbon sugar RuBP, eventually producing glucose. It does not directly need light but depends on products of the light reaction.

passages.title: Photolysis of Water
passages.text: Photolysis is the light-driven splitting of water molecules during the light reactions of photosynthesis. It occurs at photosystem II and produces oxygen gas, hydrogen ions (protons) and electrons. The oxygen released into the atmosphere during photosynthesis comes from water, not from carbon dioxide.

passages.title: Stomata and Gas Exchange
passages.text: Stomata are tiny pores mainly on the underside of leaves, each bordered by two guard cells that control their opening and closing. Carbon dioxide enters and oxygen and water vapour leave through the stomata. Guard cells regulate the pore to balance photosynthesis with water loss through transpiration.

passages.title: Limiting Factors of Photosynthesis
passages.text: The rate of photosynthesis is controlled by limiting factors: light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature. When one factor is in short supply it limits the rate even if the others are plentiful. For example, on a bright warm day the rate is often limited by carbon dioxide concentration.

passages.title: ATP and NADPH
passages.text: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the energy currency of the cell, and NADPH is a reduced electron carrier. Both are produced in the light-dependent reactions and are consumed in the Calvin cycle to convert carbon dioxide into glucose. ATP provides chemical energy while NADPH provides reducing power.

passages.title: C3, C4 and CAM Plants
passages.text: C3 plants fix carbon dioxide directly through the Calvin cycle and are common in cool climates. C4 plants such as maize and sugarcane first fix CO2 into a 4-carbon compound to reduce photorespiration in hot climates. CAM plants such as cacti open their stomata at night to conserve water in arid conditions.

passages.title: Importance of Photosynthesis
passages.text: Photosynthesis produces the oxygen we breathe and the glucose that forms the base of food chains. It removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, helping regulate climate, and stores solar energy in chemical bonds that support nearly all ecosystems on Earth.

passages.title: Raw Materials of Photosynthesis
passages.text: The raw materials needed for photosynthesis are carbon dioxide, absorbed from the air through stomata, and water, absorbed by the roots and transported through the xylem to the leaves. Sunlight and chlorophyll are also essential requirements though not consumed as raw materials.

passages.title: Where Photosynthesis Occurs
passages.text: Photosynthesis mainly occurs in the mesophyll cells of leaves, which are rich in chloroplasts. The leaf is well adapted for photosynthesis with a broad flat surface to capture light, thin structure for gas diffusion, and a network of veins to transport water and sugars.

passages.title: Photosynthetic Pigments
passages.text: Photosynthetic pigments include chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, carotenoids and xanthophylls. Each absorbs different wavelengths of light. Accessory pigments capture wavelengths that chlorophyll a cannot and pass the energy on, increasing the overall efficiency of light capture.

passages.title: Photophosphorylation
passages.text: Photophosphorylation is the synthesis of ATP using light energy during the light reactions. In non-cyclic photophosphorylation electrons flow from water through photosystems II and I to NADP+, producing ATP, NADPH and oxygen. In cyclic photophosphorylation electrons return to photosystem I and only ATP is made.

qa.question: What is photosynthesis?
qa.answer: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants convert light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose, using carbon dioxide and water and releasing oxygen.

qa.question: Write the balanced equation for photosynthesis.
qa.answer: 6CO2 + 6H2O + light energy -> C6H12O6 + 6O2.

qa.question: What is the role of chlorophyll in photosynthesis?
qa.answer: Chlorophyll is the green pigment that absorbs light energy (mainly blue and red light) needed to drive photosynthesis.

qa.question: Where does photosynthesis take place?
qa.answer: Photosynthesis takes place in the chloroplasts, mostly in the mesophyll cells of leaves.

qa.question: What are the light-dependent reactions?
qa.answer: The light-dependent reactions occur in the thylakoid membranes where light splits water (photolysis), releasing oxygen and producing ATP and NADPH.

qa.question: What happens in the Calvin cycle?
qa.answer: The Calvin cycle occurs in the stroma and uses ATP and NADPH to fix carbon dioxide into glucose using the enzyme RuBisCO.

qa.question: What is photolysis?
qa.answer: Photolysis is the light-driven splitting of water molecules during the light reactions, producing oxygen, protons and electrons.

qa.question: What are stomata and what is their function?
qa.answer: Stomata are tiny pores on leaves controlled by guard cells; they allow carbon dioxide in and oxygen and water vapour out.

qa.question: What are the limiting factors of photosynthesis?
qa.answer: The main limiting factors are light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature.

qa.question: Where does the oxygen released in photosynthesis come from?
qa.answer: The oxygen comes from the splitting of water molecules during photolysis, not from carbon dioxide.

qa.question: What is the difference between C3 and C4 plants?
qa.answer: C3 plants fix CO2 directly through the Calvin cycle, while C4 plants first fix CO2 into a 4-carbon compound to reduce photorespiration in hot climates.

qa.question: What are the raw materials required for photosynthesis?
qa.answer: The raw materials are carbon dioxide from the air and water absorbed by the roots; light and chlorophyll are also required.

qa.question: What is the function of ATP and NADPH in photosynthesis?
qa.answer: ATP provides chemical energy and NADPH provides reducing power; both are made in the light reactions and used in the Calvin cycle.

qa.question: Why is photosynthesis important?
qa.answer: It produces oxygen, forms the base of food chains, and removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, storing solar energy as chemical energy.

qa.question: What is the role of the chloroplast?
qa.answer: The chloroplast is the organelle that houses chlorophyll, thylakoids (grana) and stroma where the light and dark reactions of photosynthesis occur.

qa.question: What are CAM plants?
qa.answer: CAM plants such as cacti open their stomata at night to fix carbon dioxide and conserve water in dry, arid conditions.

qa.question: What is photophosphorylation?
qa.answer: Photophosphorylation is the light-driven synthesis of ATP during the light reactions of photosynthesis.

qa.question: Which pigments take part in photosynthesis?
qa.answer: Chlorophyll a and b are the main pigments, along with accessory pigments such as carotenoids and xanthophylls.

qa.question: Why do plants appear green?
qa.answer: Plants appear green because chlorophyll reflects green light while absorbing blue and red light for photosynthesis.

qa.question: True or False: The oxygen released in photosynthesis comes from carbon dioxide.
qa.answer: False. The oxygen released comes from the splitting of water during photolysis.
